title: Feedback: How to Make Dylan Wiliam Happy
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles takes the three principles in Dylan Wiliam's introduction to the EEF feedback report and turns each into a concrete visualiser routine for English lessons. Task design comes first, with meaningful writing tasks that generate usable evidence. Feed-forward becomes a comparison of excellent and good models, and students then write their own piece before trying a similar task. Opting in is secured by showing one or two students' work under the visualiser each time, which makes improvement visible and praise genuine. He argues this also replaces after-lesson marking, and closes with a list of consequences, including concrete improvements rather than vague comments like add more detail.
points: Poor feedback usually traces back to poor task design, because the task never elicited evidence worth responding to.
Feedback should improve the learner rather than the work, so comparing models and rewriting live is preferred to marking after the fact.
Routinely showing student work under a visualiser makes feedback an opportunity rather than a threat and so wins buy-in.
Real tasks, such as full essays and student-written poems, make students better writers than exam-format extracts do.
The visualiser routine reduces marking because improvements are made in the lesson and misconceptions seen are relevant to many students.
quotes: The reason that effective feedback requires careful preparation is because the quality of feedback that a teacher can provide depends crucially on the quality of the evidence about learners’ achievement that is available. If a teacher cannot think of what to say to a student—having seen the student’s work—then the fault is most likely that the questions, task, or activities that were assigned were not designed with a view to giving feedback in the first place. The starting point for effective feedback is eliciting the right evidence.

The main role of feedback, at least in schools, is to improve the learner, not the work. The idea is that, after feedback, students will be able to do better at some point in the future on tasks they have not yet attempted.
Every time students do any writing in your lesson, you will Show Call one or two under the visualiser. None of them will want to be exposed, so they will nearly all try really hard.

Even if they have no interest in your task, they will have an interest in not looking like an idiot. And, because they know what you are looking for, it is far easier for them to commit and act on the feedback you and/or their peers give.

Because students are Show Called under the visualiser for every written activity, feedback stops being a threat, but an opportunity to show that you have learned something. Praise, praise, meaningful praise. Buy in.

If you are always choosing real tasks - actual essays rather than starting with the extract - proper thesis statements and conclusions - actual story writing rather than extensive description - writing a personal response to poems, rather than comparing them - writing their own poems and annotating them for 3 key things they were trying to achieve, rather than writing 20 annotations slaughtering a studied poem … so students will actually improve as students of English. They will simply become better writers, for life.
